{{short description|Gives the total power radiated by an accelerating, nonrelativistic point charge}}
{{confuse|text=the phenomenon in nuclear magnetic resonance known as [[Larmor precession]]}}
[[Image:Montreal-tower-top.thumb2.jpg|thumb|right|250px|A [[Yagi–Uda antenna]]. Radio waves can be radiated from an antenna by accelerating electrons in the antenna. This is a [[Coherence (physics)|coherent]] process, so the total power radiated is proportional to the square of the number of electrons accelerating.]]
In [[electrodynamics]], the '''Larmor formula''' is used to calculate the total [[Power (physics)|power]] radiated by a nonrelativistic point charge as it accelerates. It was first derived by [[Joseph Larmor]] in 1897,<ref>{{cite journal | doi = 10.1080/14786449708621095 | volume=44 | issue=271 | title=LXIII.On the theory of the magnetic influence on spectra; and on the radiation from moving ions | year=1897 | journal=Philosophical Magazine |series= 5 | pages=503–512 | last=Larmor | first = J| url=https://zenodo.org/record/1431241 }} Formula is mentioned in the text on the last page.</ref> in the context of the [[wave theory of light]].

When any charged particle (such as an [[electron]], a [[proton]], or an [[ion]]) accelerates, energy is radiated in the form of [[electromagnetic wave]]s. For a particle whose velocity is small relative to the [[speed of light]] (i.e., nonrelativistic), the total power that the particle radiates (when considered as a point charge) can be calculated by the Larmor formula:
<math display="block">\begin{align}
P &= \frac{2}{3} \frac{q^2}{ 4 \pi \varepsilon_0 c} \left(\frac{\dot v}{c}\right)^2 = \frac{2}{3} \frac{q^2 a^2}{ 4 \pi \varepsilon_0 c^3} \\[0.6ex]
&= \frac{q^2 a^2}{6 \pi \varepsilon_0 c^3} = \mu_0 \frac{q^2 a^2}{6 \pi c} & \text{ (SI units)} \\[1.5ex]
P &= \frac{2}{3} \frac{q^2 a^2}{c^3} & \text{ (cgs units)}
\end{align}</math>
where <math> \dot v </math> or <math> a </math> is the [[proper acceleration]], <math> q </math> is the charge, <math> c </math> is the speed of light, and <math>\mu_0=1/\varepsilon_0c^2</math> is the [[vacuum permeability]].<ref>{{cite book |last1=Lorentz |first1=Hendrik Antoon |title=The theory of electrons and its applications to the phenomena of light and radiant heat |date=1909 |publisher=B.G. Teubner |location=Leipzig |pages=49–52 |author1-link=Hendrik Lorentz}}</ref> A relativistic generalization is given by the [[Liénard–Wiechert potential]]s.

In either unit system, the power radiated by a single electron can be expressed in terms of the [[classical electron radius]] and [[electron mass]] as:
<math display="block"> P = \frac{2}{3} \frac{m_e r_e a^2}{c} </math>

One implication is that an electron orbiting around a nucleus, as in the [[Bohr model]], should lose energy, fall to the nucleus and the atom should collapse. This puzzle was not solved until [[Quantum mechanics|quantum theory]] was introduced.

== Derivation==
To calculate the power radiated by a point charge <math>q</math> at a position <math>\mathbf{r}(t)</math>, with a velocity, <math>\mathbf{v}(t),</math> we integrate the [[Poynting vector]] over the surface of a sphere of radius ''R'', to get:<ref>{{cite arXiv |title=Electromagnetic Power Emitted by an Accelerating Point Charge |year=2021 |pages=1–5 |last=Franklin |first=Jerrold |class=physics.class-ph |eprint=2103.09317}}</ref>
<math display="block">
P = \frac{c R^2}{4\pi}\oint \mathbf{\hat{r}}\cdot[\mathbf E(\mathbf r,t)\times\mathbf B(\mathbf r,t)]d\Omega.</math>
The electric and magnetic fields are given  by the Liénard–Wiechert field equations,
<math display="block">\begin{align}
\mathbf{E}(\mathbf{r},t)
&= \frac{q \left(\mathbf{\hat r}_r - \boldsymbol{\beta}_r\right)}{r_r^2\gamma_r^2 {\left(1 - \mathbf{\hat r_r} \cdot \boldsymbol{\beta}_r\right)} ^3}
 + \frac{q}{c} \; \frac{\mathbf\hat{r}_r \times \left[\left(\mathbf{\hat{r}}_r - \boldsymbol{\beta}_r\right) \times \dot\boldsymbol{\beta}_r\right]} {r_r {\left(1 - \mathbf{\hat{r}}_r \cdot \boldsymbol{\beta}_r\right)}^3}
\\[1ex]
\mathbf{B}(\mathbf{r},t) &= \hat{\mathbf{r}} \times\mathbf{E}(\mathbf{r},t).
\end{align}</math>
The radius vector, <math>{\mathbf r}_r</math>, is the distance from the charged particle's position at the [[retarded time]] to the point of observation of the electromagnetic fields at the present time, <math>\boldsymbol{\beta}</math> is the charge's velocity divided by <math>c</math>, <math>\dot{\boldsymbol{\beta}}</math> is the charge's acceleration divided by <math>c</math>, and <math> \gamma = (1 - \beta^2 )^{-1/2} </math>. The variables, <math>{\mathbf r}_r</math>, <math>\boldsymbol{\beta}_r</math>, <math>\gamma_r</math>, and <math>{\mathbf a}_r</math> are all  evaluated at the retarded time, <math>t_r = t - r_r/c</math>.

We make a [[Lorentz transformation]] to the [[rest frame]] of the point charge where <math>\mathbf v'=0</math>, and
<math display="block">\begin{align}
\mathbf{a'}_\parallel &= \mathbf{a}_\parallel\gamma^3, &
\mathbf a'_\perp &= \mathbf{a}_\perp\gamma^2.
\end{align}</math>
Here, <math>{\mathbf a'}_\parallel</math> is the rest frame acceleration parallel to <math>\mathbf v</math>, and <math>\mathbf a'_\perp</math> is the rest frame acceleration perpendicular to <math>\mathbf v</math>.

We integrate the rest frame Poynting vector over the surface of a sphere of radius ''R''<nowiki/>', to get.
<math display="block">
P' = \frac{c R'^2}{4\pi} \oint \mathbf{\hat r}' \cdot \left[\mathbf{E}'(\mathbf{r}', t') \times \mathbf{B}'(\mathbf{r}',t')\right] d\Omega',</math>
We take the limit <math>R' \to 0.</math> In this limit, <math>t'_r = t'</math>, and <math>{\mathbf a'}_r={\mathbf a'}, </math> so the [[electric field]] is given by
<math display="block">\mathbf{E}'(\mathbf{r}',t') = \frac{q \mathbf{\hat{r}}'}{r'^2} + \frac{q \left[\mathbf{\hat{r}}' \left(\mathbf{\hat{r}}' \cdot \mathbf{a}'\right) - \mathbf{a}'\right]}{c^2 r'},
</math>
with all variables evaluated at the present time.

Then, the [[surface integral]] for the radiated power reduces to
<math display="block">P' = \frac{q^2}{4\pi c^3} \oint{\mathbf\hat r'} \cdot \left[ \mathbf{a}' \times \left(\hat{\mathbf{r}}' \times \mathbf{a}'\right) \right] d\Omega'
= \frac{2 q^2 a'^2}{3c^3}.</math>
The radiated power can be put back in terms of the original acceleration in the [[moving frame]], to give
<math display="block">P' = \frac{2q^2}{3c^3} \left(a^2_\parallel \gamma^6 + a^2_\perp \gamma^4\right) = \frac{2q^2 \gamma^6}{3c^3} \left[a^2 - {\left(\mathbf{v} \times \mathbf{a}/c\right)}^2\right].</math>
The variables in this equation are in the original moving frame, but the rate of energy emission on the left hand side of the equation is still given in terms of the rest frame variables. However, the right-hand side will be shown below to be a Lorentz invariant, so radiated power can be Lorentz transformed to the moving frame, finally giving
<math display="block">P = \frac{2 q^2 \gamma^4}{3c^3} \left(a^2_\parallel\gamma^2 + a_{\perp}^2\right)
= \frac{2q^2 \gamma^6}{3c^3} \left[a^2 - {\left(\mathbf{v} \times \mathbf{a}/c\right)}^2\right].</math>
This result (in two forms) is the same as Liénard's relativistic extension<ref>{{cite journal |last=Liénard |first=Alfred-Marie |year=1898 |title=Champ électrique et magnétique produit par une charge électrique concentrée en un point et animée d'un movement quelconque |journal=Eclairage Electr.16,5–14 |volume=16}}</ref> of Larmor's formula, and is given here with all variables at the present time.
Its nonrelativistic reduction reduces to Larmor's original formula.

For high-energies, it appears that the power radiated for acceleration parallel to the velocity is a factor <math>\gamma^2</math> larger than that for perpendicular acceleration.   However, writing the Liénard formula in terms of the velocity gives a misleading implication. In terms of momentum instead of velocity, the Liénard formula becomes

<math display="block">P = \frac{2q^2}{3c^3m^2} \left[\left(\frac{d\mathbf p}{dt}\right)^2_\parallel+\gamma^2\left(\frac{d\mathbf p}{dt}\right)^2_\perp\right].</math>

This shows that the power emitted for <math>d\mathbf{p}/dt</math> perpendicular to the velocity is larger by a factor of <math>\gamma^2</math> than the power for <math>d\mathbf{p}/dt</math> parallel to the velocity. This results in radiation damping being negligible for linear accelerators, but a limiting factor  for circular accelerators.

===Covariant form===
The radiated power is actually a [[Lorentz scalar]], given in covariant form as

<math display="block">P = -\frac{2}{3} \frac{q^2}{m^2c^3} \frac{dp_{\mu}}{d\tau} \frac{dp^{\mu}}{d\tau}.</math>

To show this, we reduce the [[four-vector]] scalar product to [[vector notation]].  We start with
<math display="block">
\frac{dp_{\mu}}{d\tau} \frac{dp^{\mu}}{d\tau}
= \gamma^2 \left[\left(\frac{dp_0}{dt}\right)^2
- \left(\frac{d\mathbf p}{dt}\right)^2\right].
</math>

The time derivatives are

<math display="block">
\frac{dp_0}{dt} = \frac{d}{dt}(m\gamma)
= m\gamma^3 v a_\parallel</math>
<math display="block">
\frac{d\mathbf p}{dt} = \frac{d}{dt} \left(m \mathbf{v} \gamma\right)
= m\gamma^3 \left(\mathbf{a}_\parallel + \mathbf{a}_\perp/\gamma^2\right).
</math>
When these derivatives are used,
we get<math display="block">\frac{dp_{\mu}}{d\tau} \frac{dp^{\mu}}{d\tau}
= - m^2\gamma^4\left(\gamma^2 \mathbf{a}_\parallel^2 + {\mathbf{a}}_\perp^2\right).</math>

With this expression for the scalar product, the manifestly invariant form for the power agrees with the vector form above, demonstrating that the radiated power is a Lorentz scalar

===Angular distribution===

The angular distribution of radiated power is given by a general formula, applicable whether or not the particle is relativistic. In CGS units, this formula is<ref>{{cite book |last=Jackson | first = John D. | title=Classical Electrodynamics | edition = 3rd | publisher=Wiley | year=1998 | isbn=0-471-30932-X}} (Section 14.2ff)</ref>
<math display="block"> P = \frac{2}{3} \frac{q^2}{m^2 c^3} {\left|\dot{\mathbf{p}}\right|}^2.</math>
<math display="block">\frac{dP}{d\Omega} = \frac{q^2}{4\pi c} \frac{\left|\mathbf{\hat{n}} \times \left[ (\mathbf{\hat{n}} - \boldsymbol{\beta}) \times \dot{\boldsymbol{\beta}} \right] \right|^2}{{\left(1 - \mathbf{\hat{n}} \cdot \boldsymbol{\beta}\right)}^5},</math>
where <math>\mathbf{\hat{n}}</math> is a [[unit vector]] pointing from the particle towards the observer. In the case of linear motion (velocity parallel to acceleration), this simplifies to{{sfn|Jackson|1998 |at=eq 14.39}}
<math display="block">\frac{dP}{d\Omega} = \frac{q^2a^2}{4\pi c^3} \frac{\sin^2 \theta}{{\left(1 - \beta \cos\theta\right)}^5},</math>
where <math>\theta</math> is the angle between the observer and the particle's motion.

===Radiation reaction===
The radiation from a charged particle carries energy and momentum. In order to satisfy energy and momentum conservation, the charged particle must experience a recoil at the time of emission. The radiation must exert an additional force on the charged particle. This force is known as [[Abraham–Lorentz force|Abraham-Lorentz force]] while its non-relativistic limit is known as the Lorentz self-force and relativistic forms are known as Lorentz-Dirac force or Abraham-Lorentz-Dirac force. The radiation reaction phenomenon is one of the key problems and consequences of the Larmor formula. According to classical electrodynamics, a charged particle produces electromagnetic radiation as it accelerates. The particle loses momentum and energy as a result of the radiation, which is carrying it away from it. The radiation response force, on the other hand, also acts on the charged particle as a result of the radiation.

The dynamics of charged particles are significantly impacted by the existence of this force. In particular, it causes a change in their motion that may be accounted for by the Larmor formula, a factor in the Lorentz-Dirac equation.

According to the Lorentz-Dirac equation, a charged particle's velocity will be influenced by a "self-force" resulting from its own radiation. Such non-physical behavior as runaway solutions, when the particle's velocity or energy become infinite in a finite amount of time, might result from this self-force.

A resolution to  the paradoxes resulting from the introduction of a self-force due to the emission of electromagnetic radiation, is that there is no self-force produced.  The acceleration of a charged particle produces electromagnetic radiation, whose outgoing energy reduces the energy  of the charged particle.  This results in 'radiation reaction' that decreases the acceleration of the charged particle, not as a self force, but just as less acceleration of the particle.<ref>{{cite journal | doi=10.1142/S0217751X23500057 | volume=38 | title=Radiation reaction on an accelerating point charge | year=2023 | journal=International Journal of Modern Physics A | pages= 350005–1–6| last = Franklin | first = Jerrold | issue=1 | article-number=2350005 | arxiv=2308.02628| bibcode=2023IJMPA..3850005F }}</ref>

===Atomic physics===
The invention of quantum physics, notably the Bohr model of the atom, was able to explain this gap between the classical prediction and the actual reality. The Bohr model proposed that transitions between distinct energy levels, which electrons could only inhabit, might account for the observed spectral lines of atoms. The wave-like properties of electrons and the idea of energy quantization were used to explain the stability of these electron orbits.

The Larmor formula can only be used for non-relativistic particles, which limits its usefulness. The [[Liénard–Wiechert potential|Liénard-Wiechert potential]] is a more comprehensive formula that must be employed for particles travelling at relativistic speeds. In certain situations, more intricate calculations including numerical techniques or perturbation theory could be necessary to precisely compute the radiation the charged particle emits.

==In special relativity==

There is an extension for Larmor formula in [[special relativity]]. The radiation power given a four-acceleration <math>a^\mu</math> would be

<math display="block">P = (q^2 / 6 \pi \varepsilon_o c^3) (a^\mu a_\mu)</math>

Lienard-Wiechert formula appears as the restriction of this equation when using a 3-acceleration vector.
